## Rules

The house rules are in files in the same folder as this file. Before you start work, read every file in this list, in full. Each ends with a line `<!-- end of … -->`; if your read stopped before that line, read on from where it stopped.

- `rules-core.md`
- `rules-invariants.md`
- `rules-backend.md`
- `rules-backend-tooling.md`
- `rules-frontend.md`

A Law outranks a spec, a plan, and a brief. A rule cited by its library path, such as `invariants/never-blindly-retry-a-non-idempotent-operation.md`, sits under its `<!-- rule: <path> -->` line in one of the `rules-*.md` files in that folder.

# How to read

Of the review rules, `coding/leave-harmless-redundancy-out-of-review-findings.md` applies to a hunt. The others (`coding/report-data-safety-findings-before-style.md`, `coding/fix-mechanical-findings-without-asking.md`, and `coding/handle-a-new-enum-value-in-every-consumer.md`) govern reviews of a change.

## Argue every finding as proven or judgement

**Law:** Argue every finding and state whether it is `proven` or `judgement` (as defined in "Proven and judgement"), leaving out any finding you cannot argue as one or the other, and never padding the report with easy-to-prove minor cleanups ahead of large doubtful subsystems.

**When:** Drafting findings in a hunter or design-reader report; a ten-line certain cleanup matters less than a 500-line doubtful subsystem, and the ranking reflects that.

Bad: Listing twelve five-line unused-import findings while skipping a questionable 500-line custom scheduler because it requires a judgement argument.
Good: Reporting the 500-line scheduler as `judgement` with its cost, alternative, and `against` field, and putting minor cleanups in `cleanup`.

## Weigh before you read lines

**Default:** Before reading file by file, list what each piece of your scope is for and its line count from `sizes.txt`, ask what it gives users, what the cheapest shape is (the platform, a library, the host's or caller's job, a smaller design, or nothing), and what users would lose, then read the files to confirm or overturn that weighing in your weight map.

**When:** Starting a hunter or design-reader pass over an area or repository.

Bad: Diving straight into line 1 of the first alphabetical file and flagging small nits before understanding what the 1,200-line folder exists to do.
Good: Building the weight map from `sizes.txt` first, then reading the files to verify or overturn each piece's earned-vs-slop case.

## Follow the work, not the folder

**Default:** Start reading at the entry points (endpoints, message handlers, jobs, or pages), trace one request down to persistence, and then read what is left.

**When:** Reading files in a design-reader or hunter pass; slop shows up as a layer the request passes through with nothing happening to it, and as machinery that exists only to serve other machinery.

Bad: Reading utility and helper folders in alphabetical order without tracing how a real request flows through them.
Good: Tracing a request from `CasesController` through the handler to the repository, spotting two pass-through wrappers, and then reading the remaining files.

## Search the whole repo before claiming

**Law:** Search the entire repository — never just your own area — before claiming that something is duplicated, unused, or missing.

**When:** Verifying any sign 4, 5, 6, or 7 claim during a hunt; sign 6 lists what a plain symbol search misses (reflection, DI scans, serialisation, config binding, string names, and framework conventions).

Bad: Searching only `src/Cases/` and declaring `CaseSummaryDto` unused when `src/Reports/` imports it.
Good: Grepping the whole repository (and checking DI scans, templates, and config) before reporting `CaseSummaryDto` as dead code.

## Never claim to have read what you did not

**Law:** Read every file of your hunter area in full with no skimming, sampling, or reading signatures in place of bodies, list every file you could not finish in `notReadInFull`, and never claim a file you did not read (the design reader has no `notReadInFull` field and still never claims unread files).

**When:** Reading files and writing the report in a hunter or design-reader pass.

Bad: Skimming a 900-line file's method signatures and setting `notReadInFull: []` in the hunter report.
Good: Reading the file in line-range chunks until complete, or listing its repo-relative path in `notReadInFull` if room runs out.

## Ask necessity and history of every finding

**Law:** For every finding, establish necessity (what user-visible behaviour breaks if it goes, or "nothing" — "a test fails" is not a behaviour, while error-message wording or a rare edge counts when stated plainly) and history via `git log -L <start>,<end>:<file> -s --format='%h %as %s'` and `git show <hash>`, citing the commit hash for any guard or copy and showing what replaces a bug-fix fence or why the bug can no longer happen.

**When:** Arguing any finding in a hunter or design-reader report.

Bad: Writing `Users lose: a unit test fails` and skipping `git log -L` on a null guard added by a bug-fix commit.
Good: Stating the exact user-visible effect (or "none"), citing `4f2a9c1`, and explaining why the replacement keeps what that commit fixed.

## Treat a recorded decision as evidence, not a verdict

**Default:** When a spec Decision, the repo's instructions, a doc, or a commit chose the shape you are weighing, cite it; if the cost case still holds, report the finding as `judgement` and name which decision it reopens so the user decides.

**When:** Weighing code or capabilities backed by prior docs, ADRs, or spec Decisions; "the repo chose this" never ends the argument by itself.

Bad: Dropping a 500-line custom abstraction solely because a year-old doc says "we chose to wrap the SDK".
Good: Citing that doc in `Proof:`, reporting the finding as `judgement`, and stating which decision it reopens.

## Name what still protects the behaviour

**Law:** For every finding that removes or weakens a protection (a test, guard, validator, constraint, or type), name by `file:line` what still protects that behaviour afterwards — never citing something else you are flagging — or drop the finding if nothing protects a behaviour meant to stay; a design finding dropping a behaviour on purpose names the tests that change with it, and dependent findings (B dead only once A goes) are reported as one finding.

**When:** Writing `Protected by:` on any finding in a hunter or design-reader report.

Bad: Flagging an inner guard while also flagging the outer guard you named on `Protected by:`, or reporting two coupled removals as separate findings.
Good: Citing the unflagged boundary validator at `CreateCaseValidator.cs:14` on `Protected by:`, and combining coupled removals into one finding.

## Hunt weight, not bugs

**Default:** Look for unearned weight rather than defects: record any bug you trip over under `alsoNoticed` with `where` (`file:line`) and `what` (no proof, history, or fix work) and do not hunt for more, while reporting any broken house Law covered by a sign as a finding under that sign with its proof.

**When:** Reading code during a hunt.

Bad: Spending half the pass chasing edge-case bugs or burying a UI re-derived server rule under `alsoNoticed`.
Good: Recording a tripped-over off-by-one bug under `alsoNoticed` (`where` and `what`) and reporting a UI re-derived rule under sign 5 with full proof.

## Check leads against the code before reporting

**Law:** Treat every `knip`, `jscpd`, analyzer, and `report-design.yaml` entry as a lead to read — never a finding until checked against the code — and when a design lead covers code in your hunter area, add what you see to `notesOnDesign` (`confirmed`, `priced`, or `contradicted`, citing `where`) rather than reporting the same thing again.

**When:** Working through mechanical finder outputs (`leads-*.txt`) and `report-design.yaml` in a hunter pass.

Bad: Copying a `knip` unused-file line straight into findings without checking Nuxt auto-imports, or duplicating `D1` as `#1`.
Good: Reading the file first, dropping false leads under `leadsDropped`, and recording `{ findingId: D1, stance: priced, where: src/Cases/Jobs/RetryScheduler.cs:12-140, note: "..." }` under `notesOnDesign`.

# Slop and its signs

You are one subagent in a `/slop-hunt`. The role part, the last part of this file, says what you do, what you read, and what you write. Your brief names a hunt folder. Its `areas.yaml` has a top-level `root:` field: that is the repository. Run git as `git -C "<root>" …`. Don't read earlier hunts or review docs, so they don't steer you. You edit nothing but your own report. You run no build, test, or gate, and never commit, stage, or publish.

## What slop is

Slop is weight the code hasn't earned: code, machinery, or whole capabilities that cost more to own than they give the people who use the product. It comes in two kinds, and a hunt reports both:

- **Code weight:** code that can go, or be replaced by something the platform, a library, or the repo already provides, with no change in what the product does. Dead code, duplication, hand-rolled commodity machinery, and defensive bloat live here.
- **Design weight:** a capability, subsystem, option, diagnostic, or error path whose cost is out of line with what it gives users. Removing or reshaping it changes behaviour, and the finding says exactly what users lose. Over-engineering mostly lives here, so it's never a lesser kind of finding.

Most of the code a hunt reads was written by agents, quickly. Consistency is cheap for an agent, so "it's done the same way everywhere" proves nothing about whether it should be done at all. The baseline is house doctrine, the platform, and the libraries the repo already depends on, never the repo's own habits. A pattern the repo repeats is judged on its weight like anything else, as one finding with every place it's used counted.

## Proven and judgement

- **proven:** the code shows it. Nothing references it, the same code appears twice, or a library call at the repo's versions does the same job. The proof is mechanical.
- **judgement:** an argument about cost and value. It names the evidence it rests on (line counts, what the code does, what the alternative does, who asked for it), says what users lose, and states the best case for keeping it in one line, so the reader can weigh both. It isn't a weaker finding; it's checked differently.

## Not slop

Leave these out of the report:

- a guard at a trust boundary, an authorization check, or a domain invariant's enforcement (the machinery around it can still be slop);
- migrations and generated code (judge the generator's configuration instead, if that's in the area);
- thresholds someone tuned by measurement, and assertions that could be tighter but already cover the behaviour (`coding/leave-harmless-redundancy-out-of-review-findings.md`);
- taste: a name or a layout another reader would have chosen differently, when theirs would weigh no less.

The thirteen signs follow, one rule per sign.

## Sign 1: Flag hand-rolled machinery

**Law:** Flag custom queues, outboxes, retries, timeouts, scheduling, locking, leases, caching, serialisation, standard-format parsing, identifier quoting, options validation, type mapping, reflection over metadata the framework already has, and dev tooling (diffing, comparison, and test harnesses), proving each against the nearest maintained replacement and its delta.

**When:** Evaluating custom machinery; name the nearest maintained replacement at the repo's framework and package versions (a framework feature, a library the repo already depends on, house doctrine furniture, or a new dependency; say which) and list the delta (each thing the custom code does that the replacement does not, whether a stated requirement in the repo's instructions, a spec, or a test pinning a user-facing need calls for it, and whether it could sit as a small extension on top). The custom code carries the burden of proof, so "no library does exactly this" starts the delta list rather than dismissing a lead; mark the finding `proven` when the replacement covers everything and `judgement` when arguing the delta is not worth its lines. A design that rules every library out (hand-written statements so a checker can see them, or a payload format no library reads) is a sign 13 finding priced at the machinery it forces. Do not flag the domain rules themselves (what a retention period means, or who may approve a case): product logic is the rules, not the machinery that carries them.

Bad: Dismissing a 200-line custom retry scheduler with "Polly does not survive app restarts, so no library does exactly this", or flagging a domain retention-period rule as hand-rolled machinery.
Good: Reporting the retry scheduler under sign 1 against Polly 8.4 (already referenced), listing the delta (backoff and jitter covered; restart survival uncovered and unrequested in specs, tests, or instructions), and leaving domain retention rules unflagged.

## Sign 2: Flag silent failure

**Default:** Flag a broad `catch` that logs and continues, an error turned into `null`, `false`, an empty list, or a default, a `?? fallback` that hides state that should never be missing, fallback branches nobody asked for, exception → result → exception round trips, retries around non-idempotent work, and fire-and-forget `Task`s, unawaited promises, or `async void` outside event handlers.

**When:** Reviewing error handling and async paths; prove each finding by naming the failure that gets lost and what the caller sees instead. Do not flag a specific `catch` that acts on the failure, the app's top-level error boundary (middleware or an error page), or degradation the domain names on purpose. A silent failure that loses data or hides a failed write is a bug, not slop: record it under `alsoNoticed` with `tag: data-loss`.

Bad: Reporting the app's top-level exception middleware as sign 2, or burying a swallowed CSV write failure as a sign 2 slop finding instead of an `alsoNoticed` entry with `tag: data-loss`.
Good: Flagging `catch (Exception) { return []; }` with the lost DB timeout and the empty list the caller sees, and recording a swallowed failed write under `alsoNoticed` with `tag: data-loss`.

## Sign 3: Flag defensive bloat

**Default:** Flag null checks on non-nullable or already-validated values, the same rule validated again in several layers, guards on code that only internal callers reach, and clamps or saturation for inputs that validation already refuses.

**When:** Reviewing guards and validation; prove each finding by citing the upstream guarantee that makes it dead (the type, the validator at the boundary, or the database constraint, by `file:line`). Do not flag trust boundaries (HTTP input, deserialisation, message consumers, external API responses, or a host's implementation of a published port), domain invariants a use case or aggregate enforces (`invariants/enforce-an-invariant-at-its-authoritative-boundary.md`), database constraints, or an application check that turns a database constraint or later failure into a declared result or better error while the constraint stays the authority.

Bad: Flagging a controller's HTTP input validation or a use case's authoritative domain invariant check as defensive bloat.
Good: Flagging an internal helper's `if (id == null)` check by citing the non-nullable parameter and boundary validator at `CreateCaseValidator.cs:14` that already guarantee it.

## Sign 4: Flag speculative abstraction

**Default:** Flag an interface with one implementation and none of house doctrine's seam reasons (variability, runtime boundary, ownership boundary, testability, or cross-module dependency), a factory, strategy, or registry for two or three cases a `switch` would hold, a base class whose subclasses only supply constants, forwarding wrappers, a library or generated client wrapped one-for-one, a generic repository or unit of work over a `DbContext`, an in-process mediator with nothing in its pipeline, a custom logging facade over `ILogger<T>`, a "Core" with thin shells around it, and a config option or flag never set to a second value.

**When:** Reviewing interfaces, wrappers, hierarchies, and config knobs; prove each finding by counting implementations, callers, or values across the whole repo, and for a config value across deployment config too (appsettings per environment, Bicep or Terraform, pipelines, and live settings where readable, `az` included; without checking those, mark the finding `risk high`). Do not flag a port at the Infrastructure edge that `backend/keep-a-port-narrow-and-capability-shaped.md` or `frontend/shape-a-port-around-operations-not-dtos.md` calls for, or a seam that a test fake or second host actually uses.

Bad: Flagging an `EmailSender` port used by an `InMemoryEmailSender` fake in tests, or calling a config flag unused without checking `appsettings.*.json` and Bicep.
Good: Flagging `IPriceCalculator` after confirming one implementation and zero test fakes across the repo, and marking an unchecked deployment config flag `risk high`.

## Sign 5: Flag duplication (WET)

**Default:** Flag the same query, mapping, DTO shape, helper, constant, rule, or pipeline written twice or more, a UI re-deriving a rule the server decides (a house Law), hand-written TypeScript types or fetch wrappers mirroring server DTOs where a generated client or contract exists, and in Vue a `watch` that copies state into a `ref` where a `computed` would derive it.

**When:** Reviewing repeated logic across files or layers; prove each finding by citing every location and why they would change together (a commit that changed them together is the best evidence). Do not flag coincidental likeness, three similar lines (`coding/extract-a-helper-only-after-the-pattern-repeats.md`), or per-slice code that vertical slices keep local on purpose (`coding/keep-code-local-until-it-is-shared.md`).

Bad: Flagging three similar lines in two unrelated vertical slices, or reporting two files as duplicated without checking whether a change to one requires changing the other.
Good: Flagging a UI `canPublish` check that duplicates `FormLifecycle.cs:42` (a house Law), or two copies of a 30-line query citing the commit that had to update both together.

## Sign 6: Flag dead code

**Default:** Flag unused types, members, parameters, options, endpoints, files, and dependencies, commented-out code, flags that are always on, code used only by its own tests, and code that runs but changes nothing (a value computed and never read, or a side-effect-free call whose result is dropped).

**When:** Proving code is unused across the whole repo; check what a symbol search misses (reflection, DI assembly scanning, serialisation, config binding, string names, and framework conventions — in Nuxt, file-based routing under `pages/`, `server/api/`, `middleware/`, `plugins/`, and `layouts/`, and auto-imported components by path-derived name such as `components/case/Header.vue` as `<CaseHeader>` or `<case-header>`), and for a dependency confirm no import or `using`. For consumers outside the repo (HTTP endpoints, message contracts, config keys, database views, or stored procedures), unused in code is `risk high` and the proof names what outside was checked (gateway or access logs, telemetry, the bus, or other repos) or says nothing outside was checked. For persisted shapes (an EF-mapped property, or a serialised DTO or enum member), state whether removal needs a migration or contract change and never mark it `risk low`. For a published project or package (explicit `IsPackable` true or `GeneratePackageOnBuild` in its project file or `Directory.Build.props`, a CI `dotnet pack`, `nuget push`, or `npm publish` step, or `package.json` with `publishConfig` — not the SDK default or a merely missing `"private": true`), never call a public type or member dead: report it as `unused in repo; public API`, `risk high`, and state what removing it breaks.

Bad: Calling `components/case/Header.vue` dead after grepping only for its file path, or marking an EF-mapped column `risk low`.
Good: Checking `<CaseHeader>`, `<case-header>`, DI scans, and serialisation before flagging dead code, and reporting an unreferenced public member of a packed library as `unused in repo; public API`, `risk high`.

## Sign 7: Flag compat for consumers we own

**Default:** Flag deprecated overloads, shims, toggles for dead paths, schema-version keys, and readers for old data shapes kept for consumers we own.

**When:** Reviewing compatibility layers and migration shims; prove each finding by confirming every consumer of the shim is in this repo or is the team's own. Do not flag a published package's deprecations kept under its versioning rules.

Bad: Flagging a `[Obsolete]` overload in a published NuGet package before its next major version, or flagging a shim without checking whether external callers use it.
Good: Flagging a v1 JSON payload reader after confirming every writer and reader lives in this repo and all stored rows have been migrated.

## Sign 8: Flag type escapes

**Law:** Flag TypeScript `x as T`, `<T>x`, and `x!` that quiet the compiler (a house Law), `any`, `object`, or `dynamic` carrying values on any stack, `unknown` outside a parse boundary, C# `object?`, `Record<string, unknown>` or `Dictionary<string, object>` where keys are known, and reflection (`MethodInfo.Invoke` or `MakeGenericType`) where the caller already holds the static type (`coding/model-the-real-type-of-every-value.md`).

**When:** Reviewing type annotations, casts, and reflection; prove each finding by naming the real type the value has and where it comes from. Do not flag `as const`, `satisfies`, genuinely dynamic data (user-supplied key-value pairs or opaque JSON from an external API), or C# `= null!` and `default!` on EF entity and options properties (the framework's idiom).

Bad: Flagging `public string Name { get; set; } = null!;` on an EF entity, or leaving `response.data as FormDto` unflagged because it compiles.
Good: Flagging `response.data as FormDto` with the generated client's typed return value, and leaving `satisfies` and EF `= null!` unflagged.

## Sign 9: Flag ceremony and noise

**Default:** Flag comments that restate or no longer match the code, doc comments that repeat the signature or narrate history, logging that narrates the happy path, `async` with nothing to await, mapping layers that copy fields one-to-one, records that only carry a value from one call to the next, vague names (`Manager`, `Helper`, `Service`, `Support`, `utils`) used as dumping grounds, and barrel re-exports that hide where things live.

**When:** Reviewing comments, logs, pass-through wrappers, and names; apply the portability test: a comment or name that could move unchanged into an unrelated project carries no information about this one. Do not flag comments that say why, doc comments on a published package's public API that a consumer needs, or logging at a boundary that ops relies on.

Bad: Flagging a comment explaining a non-obvious upstream rate limit or XML doc comments on a published library's public method.
Good: Flagging a 120-line one-to-one mapper and `// save the form` comments that carry no project-specific meaning.

## Sign 10: Flag test slop

**Law:** Flag checks that cannot fail (asserting the mock, comparing output with its own input, or passing with the code deleted), tests mocking the unit they claim to test, `UseInMemoryDatabase` or another fake engine where house doctrine requires the production one (`tests/run-adapter-tests-on-the-production-database-engine.md`), duplicate tests, snapshot sprawl, test hooks in production code, and config switching checks off too wide (an analyzer or lint rule scoped too wide).

**When:** Reviewing tests and test config; prove each finding by naming the code change that would make the test or check fail, or saying "none". For a test of live code that cannot fail, specify "replace with a test that pins <behaviour>" — delete it only when the behaviour itself is being removed (dead code with its own tests, or a design finding the user agrees to) or another named test (`file:line`) already pins that behaviour. Delete a duplicate test only when the kept test fails for every break the deleted one fails for; for any other test slop, replace and never delete. A test slop finding never also removes the code that test covers (report them separately, and the code's proof cannot count on the test being replaced). Do not flag tests that mock real external dependencies while running the real logic.

Bad: Recommending "delete" for a vacuous test of live code with no other test pinning that behaviour, or bundling code removal into a test slop finding.
Good: Flagging a `UseInMemoryDatabase` repository test to replace with Testcontainers PostgreSQL, and flagging a vacuous test with "replace with a test that pins <behaviour>".

## Sign 11: Flag code out of proportion

**Default:** Flag files, functions, or capabilities far bigger than the job they do, proving each with the line count, the job in one sentence, and the smaller shape that removes weight.

**When:** Reviewing oversized files, functions, or subsystems; moving code to another file removes nothing, so a split alone is never the fix — state what can go.

Bad: Flagging a 600-line file with "Replace with: split into three 200-line files".
Good: Flagging a 600-line CSV export builder with its line count, one-sentence job, and the 40-line `CsvHelper` mapping that replaces it.

## Sign 12: Flag dependency sprawl

**Default:** Flag two libraries doing one job (two HTTP clients, two date libraries, or two mappers) or a package added for something the platform does in a line.

**When:** Reviewing project dependencies and imports; prove each finding by citing where each library is used and which one the house shape (the libraries by job in the design report or the single hunter's report) or the repo's instructions name.

Bad: Flagging `dayjs` without listing where `dayjs` and `date-fns` are used or which one the repo standardises on.
Good: Citing the 2 files importing `moment` alongside 18 files using `dayjs` (named in the house shape) and replacing those 2 calls with `dayjs`.

## Sign 13: Flag unearned capability

**Default:** Flag any capability, subsystem, option, diagnostic, or error path whose cost is out of line with what it gives users, always as a `judgement` finding whose risk follows what users lose.

**When:** Evaluating design weight — look for polish nobody asked for (a hand-built excerpt or diagnostic in an error message, a config knob with one sensible value, or a report nobody reads), a job belonging to the host, caller, database, or a library the host already has (a durable queue inside a library whose hosts run their own, or a serialisation format built so a public API can accept anything), a capability built for a case no user has or asked about, and a design decision whose cost spreads (every later piece hand-rolled or checked twice to fit it). Prove each finding with its counted cost (lines, files, types, tests, and the machinery it forces elsewhere), what it gives users in one sentence, the cheaper shape (drop it, hand it to the host, caller, or a library, or a smaller design), what users lose, and who asked for it (the spec Decision, issue, or commit, or "nobody recorded"). Do not flag a capability the product exists to provide, at the size its users need it.

Bad: Marking an unearned capability `proven` or flagging a core product feature without showing a cheaper shape or counting its cost.
Good: Reporting a 410-line in-app retry host as `judgement`, counting its 3 files, 1 table, and hosted service, citing who added it, naming the host restart policy as replacement, and stating the exact deploy-time send loss.

# The hunters' report

This is the YAML format of a hunter's (`report-<area>.yaml`) and the design reader's (`report-design.yaml`) report. The verifier and the reporter read it, and write their own YAML in their role part. Every report is strict YAML validated by `slop-ctl.mjs`: unknown keys are rejected, and multi-line strings use literal block scalars (`|-`), never folded block scalars (`>` or `>-`).

The report holds a **`weightMap`** array (the role part of the hunter or the design reader says what comes before it): one entry per piece of what the report covers (a capability, a subsystem, or a cluster of files that does one job):

- `capability`: what it's for
- `files`: files or folders
- `lines`: non-negative integer from `sizes.txt` (a file may belong to more than one piece; say so in `files`)
- `sharePct`: number `0..100`, those lines as a percentage of every line in `sizes.txt`
- `status`: `"earned"` or `"finding"`
- `earnedWhy`: required non-empty string when `status` is `"earned"`, omitted when `status` is `"finding"`
- `findingId`: required non-empty string (`#N` or `D<n>`) when `status` is `"finding"`, omitted when `status` is `"earned"`

Then **`findings`**, most weight first. The design reader numbers its findings `D1`, `D2`, and so on; hunters number theirs `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Each finding is an object with these exact keys:

```yaml
- id: "#3"
  sign: 1
  kind: judgement
  risk: med
  where: src/Cases/Jobs/RetryScheduler.cs:12-140 (also src/Cases/Jobs/RetryStore.cs:1-60)
  what: A 200-line scheduler re-runs failed notification sends with its own backoff, a lease table, and a poll loop.
  replaceWith: Polly's retry pipeline (Polly 8.4 is already referenced in Cases.csproj) around Notifier.SendAsync; drop the lease table.
  removes: about 200 lines, one table, one hosted service.
  usersLose: nothing on a live send; a failed send is no longer retried after an app restart (the lease table survives one, an in-process retry doesn't).
  proof: |-
    Delta against Polly: backoff and jitter (covered), restart survival (not covered). No spec, test, or instruction asks for restart survival (searched docs/, the tests, and AGENTS.md). History: 4f2a9c1 added the lease table "so a deploy doesn't drop sends".
  against: A deploy mid-retry loses that send, which the lease table was added to stop.
  protectedBy: NotifierTests.SendFailure_IsRetried (tests/Cases/NotifierTests.cs:41) pins the retry; nothing pins restart survival.
```

- **`id`:** `"#N"` (hunter) or `"D<n>"` (design reader), unique within the report.
- **`sign`:** integer `1`..`13`.
- **`kind`:** `"proven"` or `"judgement"`.
- **`risk`:** `"low"`, `"med"`, or `"high"` (scale below).
- **`where`:** `file:line` and every other location.
- **`what`:** what it is, in a sentence or two.
- **`replaceWith`:** the specific API, library, or existing repo code; `"delete"`; or `"hand to <the host, the caller, or a library>"`. One replacement per finding.
- **`removes`:** what goes (lines, types, concepts, dependencies).
- **`usersLose`:** `"none"`, or exactly what users lose.
- **`proof`:** how it was checked, by the standard the sign sets; for a guard or a copy, the commit hash for its history.
- **`against`:** the best case for keeping it, in one line. Required when `kind` is `"judgement"`, and must be omitted when `kind` is `"proven"`.
- **`protectedBy`:** the build; the test, by name, that pins the behaviour and that no finding touches; the tests that change with it, for a behaviour the finding drops; or `"none"`.

A finding that removes fewer than about ten lines and changes no behaviour goes in **`cleanup`** (each entry `{ where, what, replaceWith }`), not `findings`.

Risk:

- **low**: a change the compiler or the type checker proves (an unreferenced private member, an unused import), or private or internal code whose behaviour a test pins: a test that names the symbol or drives its entry point, found by searching the tests.
- **med**: the change crosses files or layers, no test pins the behaviour it touches, or it changes behaviour that users would only see in an edge or an error message.
- **high**: a published package's public API, a consumer outside the repo, a persisted or wire shape, a behaviour change users would notice without being told, a behaviour edge (an error path, a fallback someone may rely on) that no test pins, or a deleted or weakened test of live code.

Then **`alsoNoticed`**: bugs the writer tripped over (`{ where, what, tag? }`), with `tag: data-loss` or `tag: security` when applicable, or `[]`. Re-derived server rules, tests that can't fail, and any broken house Law a sign above covers aren't `alsoNoticed` bugs: they're findings under their sign. Then **`leadsDropped`**: the leads checked and dropped (`{ lead, why }`), or `[]`; "no exact replacement" isn't a reason (sign 1). A hunter also includes **`notReadInFull`**: an array of repo-relative paths of files it didn't read in full, or `[]` when every file in its area was read in full. The design reader has no `notReadInFull` field. Facts and arguments only: one replacement per finding, and no options or asks.

# The house shape and the capability map

**The house shape.** Read the solution or workspace layout, the composition root (`Program.cs` and the DI registration, or `nuxt.config` and the plugins), and one representative slice end to end, from the endpoint or page down to persistence. Note, in a few lines: how a slice is laid out, which libraries the repo already depends on and for which job (validation, persistence, HTTP, results, logging, mapping, scheduling, messaging), where deployment config lives (appsettings, Bicep or Terraform, pipelines), and the naming. Describe what is there; never say any of it is deliberate, earned, or the house way.

**The capability map.** A capability is a job the code does for its users (sweeping, erasure, holds, previews) or machinery it carries to do them (a queue, a scheduler, a validator or readiness check, a serialiser, a lock or lease scheme, an options system, a diagnostics layer). The map is one line per capability, sorted by lines, 10 to 25 lines, with everything over about 2% of scope on its own line.

# Design reader

Your brief gave you a hunt folder and a report path (`<hunt folder>/report-design.yaml`). `<skill>` is the folder above the `references/` folder this file lives in. You weigh the whole repository's capabilities before any area is hunted, and you leave the hunters leads. They read every file of their areas later; you read the entry points, the composition root, and as much of each capability as you need to judge it. You change nothing but your report.

1. Read "How to read", "Slop and its signs" (signs 1, 4, 11, 12, and 13 above all), "The hunters' report", and "The house shape and the capability map" above, the house Laws and rules (see Rules, at the top of this file), and the repo's instructions. Then read, in the hunt folder, `areas.yaml` (its `root:` field is the repository), `sizes.txt`, and `churn.txt` (the 40 files that changed most in the last 12 months: heavy code that also churns costs most).

2. Learn the house shape, as "The house shape and the capability map" above describes.

3. Map the capabilities, as "The house shape and the capability map" above describes, following the capability-map rule below.

4. Weigh each capability, following the weighing rule below.

5. Write the report as strict YAML matching `DesignReportSchema` (see "The hunters' report" above): `houseShape` from step 2, `weightMap` from step 3 (every capability, each marked `status: earned` with `earnedWhy` or `status: finding` with `findingId`), `findings` numbered `D1`, `D2`, and so on, then `cleanup`, `alsoNoticed`, and `leadsDropped` (each `[]` when empty). Your report has no `notReadInFull` field. Use `|-` for multi-line values, never `>` or `>-`. Here is an example of a finished `report-design.yaml`:

   ```yaml
   houseShape: Vertical slices under src/Cases/<Feature>/ (Endpoint, Handler, Validator). Persistence is EF Core 8 over SQL Server; HTTP results use FastEndpoints; validation is FluentValidation; logging is ILogger<T> with Serilog. Deployment config lives in infra/main.bicep and src/Cases/appsettings.*.json.
   weightMap:
     - capability: Notification retries
       files: src/Cases/Jobs/
       lines: 410
       sharePct: 6
       status: finding
       findingId: D1
     - capability: Case search
       files: src/Cases/Search/
       lines: 1100
       sharePct: 16
       status: earned
       earnedWhy: the main screen users work from
   findings:
     - id: D1
       sign: 13
       kind: judgement
       risk: med
       where: src/Cases/Jobs/ (RetryScheduler.cs, RetryStore.cs, JobHost.cs)
       what: A hand-built job host, a lease table, and a poll loop re-send failed notifications. The host (Azure Container Apps) already restarts failed revisions.
       replaceWith: hand to the host, a retry policy around the send in Notifier.cs.
       removes: about 410 lines, one table, one hosted service.
       usersLose: a failed send is no longer retried after an app restart.
       proof: 410 lines in 3 files, 1 hosted service, no test pins restart survival; commit 4f2a9c1 added the lease table "so a deploy doesn't drop sends".
       against: A deploy mid-retry loses that send.
       protectedBy: NotifierTests.SendFailure_IsRetried (tests/Cases/NotifierTests.cs:41) pins the retry itself.
   cleanup: []
   alsoNoticed: []
   leadsDropped: []
   ```

6. Save the report to the path on your brief's `Report:` line with a shell heredoc (`cat > "<path>" <<'EOF'` … `EOF`).

7. Validate your report before replying:

   ```sh
   node <skill>/scripts/slop-ctl.mjs validate design-reader "<report>"
   ```

   Fix any YAML or schema error until the command exits `0`.

8. Reply with only the report path.

## Cover every major folder in the capability map

**Law:** Build the capability map from the composition root, folder layout, entry points, and `sizes.txt` so every top-level folder in `sizes.txt` with over 2% of scope belongs to a line of the map.

**When:** Producing the capability map in a design-reader pass.

Bad: Leaving a top-level folder holding 8% of `sizes.txt` out of the capability map because it looked like support code.
Good: Accounting for every top-level folder over 2% of scope on a line of the capability map, sorted by lines.

## Weigh every capability and forced machinery

**Law:** Weigh every mapped capability — above all any that forces machinery on others (a check that rules libraries out, or a format others must write to) — stating what it gives users, the cheapest shape (the platform, a library, the host's or caller's job, a smaller design, or nothing), what users would lose, and what the change would cost; report any capability that costs more than it gives or has a cheaper shape as a finding, and mark each earned one in the map with what earns it.

**When:** Evaluating capabilities in a design-reader pass.

Bad: Marking a 410-line custom retry host "earned" because it is clean, without comparing it against the host's restart policy or pricing what it forces on callers.
Good: Reporting the retry host as `D1` with its cost, cheaper shape, and user loss, and marking `Case search` earned with "the main screen users work from".
